newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch unemployment fall shows job creation success.
newsitem.headline: Dutch unemployment fall shows job creation success.

text.p: Dutch unemployment levels surprised many by falling in the months December to February, but economists said it was representative of a healthy Dutch economy and its success at job creation.
"It is a surprise, there is a fairly wide margin of error,.. but it seems the rise in the number of jobs may be taking some effect," said Nico Klene, economist at ABN AMRO Bank.

Non-seasonally adjusted unemployment fell to an average of 429,000 or 6.4 percent of the labour force in the December-February period from 437,000 (6.5 percent) in November-January, the Central Bureau of Statistics said on Wednesday.
The seasonally adjusted figure was down to 417,000 in December-February (6.2 percent of the workforce) from 429,000 (6.4 percent) in November-January.
Economists polled by Reuters had expected a 1,000 rise in the non-adjusted figure and a 2,000 fall in the adjusted number.

"The Netherlands has benefited from a policy of wage restraint and the reduction in working hours. Sooner or later that must lead to a fall in unemployment," said Fred Pallada, head of country analysis at ING Netherlands.
The Dutch have been particularly successful at creating jobs, manifestly more so than their German neighbours.

In 1996, the number of people in work in the Netherlands grew by 124,000, or about two percent. The key to the success has been economic growth, fueled by rising consumption, combined with wage restraint and workers' adaptability.
"The Dutch labour market is more flexible, with more part-time and more temporary jobs," said Aline Schuiling, economist at merchant bank MeesPierson.
However, during 1996, unemployment only fell by 40,000.
So while economists hoped Wednesday's figures were the start of a longer term trend, they were wary of reading too much into today's lean figures.
Some said the unemployment fall could be the result of short-term fluctuations in the number of people seeking work.
"The problem is that the labour supply is the most unpredictable factor. Job creation is very good, but the labour supply has grown at a very high rate," said Schuiling.
She said women had noticeably entered the labour market last summer, lengthening the job queues.
Indeed, the Netherlands' very success at creating jobs may have stifled its attempts at trimming unemployment.
"Whenever there are new jobs, more people show up," said Pallada.
